seo_title: Ogopogo: Okanagan Lake monster sightings and the films
seo_desc: The Ogopogo story from the Syilx spirit of Okanagan Lake to the 1924 song, the Folden and Chaplin films, and what the skeptics found when they measured the footage.
summary: Canada's famous lake serpent of Okanagan Lake, BC: a Syilx lake spirit, a music hall song, and four films that don't hold up as well as people think.
body: Ogopogo is the name settlers gave the serpent of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. Long before that the Syilx Okanagan people knew the being as n'x̌x̌aitkʷ, a spirit of the lake tied to Rattlesnake Island and the cliffs at Squally Point.

The usual description is 40 to 50 ft of dark, smooth body moving in a row of humps. That sounds a lot like a plesiosaur, which is why the story travelled, but the best-known films of it turn out to be a lot smaller and a lot closer to shore than the people who shot them thought.

Nobody has produced a body, a clear photograph or a sonar hit that settles it. The honest read is that Okanagan Lake has otters, beavers, old log booms and a lot of deep cold water, and a person squinting into a glare can turn any of that into a monster.

p: Okanagan Lake is 127 km long and 232 m deep at its deepest, one of five big fjord lakes strung down the valley. The Syilx have lived on it since long before anyone was writing things down, and their account of the lake includes a being with real power. The Secwepemc and Syilx called it Naitaka, and the word n'ha-a-itk gets translated as water demon, water god or sacred creature of the water depending on who you ask.

In the version that got written down by settlers, Naitaka demanded an offering before you crossed. People sacrificed small animals at the water before setting out. The story of chief Timbasket is the cautionary one, and he refused to make the offering, told everyone the demon wasn't real, and paddled out with his family. According to the account, the lake whipped up, the canoe was pulled under and nobody came back. In 1855 a settler named John MacDougal said his horses were dragged into the water, and that he cut the line to keep his own canoe from going with them.

Here's the part most retellings leave out. Pat Raphael of Westbank First Nation says the demon framing came out of bad translation between early settlers and the Okanagan people. To the Syilx the being is a sacred spirit that protects the valley. Jordan Coble of Westbank First Nation makes the same point from the other direction, that this is a being to respect rather than fear, and that n'ha-a-itk covers the creature and everything else in the valley, not one animal in the water. Knowledge keeper Richard Armstrong in Penticton has said plainly that for his people the lake creature is an accepted part of life, not folklore to be argued about. I'm not going to tell anyone their tradition is wrong.

sections.h: How a lake monster got a music hall name
p: Ogopogo is not an old name. Historian Mark Orkin traced it to a night in 1924 when a British music hall song turned up in Vernon, BC. The chorus was about a creature whose mother was an earwig and whose father was a whale, with a little bit of head and hardly any tail, and Ogopogo was his name. That's the whole origin. Somebody sang a silly song in a hall and the lake's monster has been called Ogopogo ever since.

Orkin also noted a 1926 piece in the Vancouver Province that claimed the name had been in use since 1912, and versions of the song did the rounds with different words. Ogopogo is a palindrome, which is too good to waste, so local lore says the creature appears the same from either end. People call it Oggy for short, and small ones are Ogopups.

The first detailed account from a settler came earlier than the song. Susan Allison, who was among the first non-native people to live in the valley, described seeing something in the lake in 1872. Settler reports build up from the 1870s on, so the creature was already a local story before it had the name everyone uses now.
Four pieces of footage carry most of the weight, and each one has been looked at by people who do this for a living.

Art Folden, 1968. Driving Highway 97 he saw something moving offshore, pulled over and shot a home movie of a long wake crossing calm water. Computer analysis of the footage concluded it was a solid three-dimensional object, which is the line you see quoted everywhere. In 2005 Benjamin Radford, Joe Nickell and John Kirk took surveyor boats out for a National Geographic Channel show called Is It Real? and measured where the thing actually was. It was much closer to shore than Folden thought, which shrinks the size and the speed. Their conclusion was a real animal, probably a water bird, an otter or a beaver, too far away to identify.

Larry Thal, 1980. About 50 tourists watched something off a Kelowna beach for roughly 45 minutes while Thal got 10 seconds of it on 8 mm film. Skeptics have suggested a pair of otters, which sounds dismissive until you see two otters swim in a line.

Ken and Clem Chaplin, 1989. The Chaplins staked out the log booms near Bear Creek with a video camera and filmed something they described as a slim serpent up to 15 ft long about 75 ft from their canoe. Ken said it slapped its tail hard enough to kill a man and then dove. It made Time magazine and Unsolved Mysteries. Local biologist Robert Lincoln said the size was probably exaggerated and the animal was likely a beaver, and Chris Bull, a former head of Fisheries and Oceans Canada, said the same thing about this kind of sighting in general. That's a sobering pair of verdicts on the best-known Ogopogo video.

Paul DeMara, 1992. He filmed something moving just under the surface at maybe 8 km/h, then a boat towing a water skier came into frame and the skier fell in right by the object. Radford again suggested otters. In 2005 Grant Fredericks, a certified forensic video analyst, said the object was very consistent with debris from a fallen tree, that it bobbed slowly, and that neither the skier nor anyone else in the boat reacted to it. A lake monster that doesn't bother a swimmer five feet away is not a lake monster.
There's also a 2008 photo from Peachland, and the usual run of phone videos since. Nothing in that pile has ever survived being examined.

Otters are the big one. River otters swim in a line, hump up and down, and at a few hundred metres they look exactly like a serpent with five humps. Beavers show up too, and Okanagan used to be a forestry lake, which means log booms and drifting deadheads, and a half-sunk log in a light chop has fooled better observers than me. Then there are the ordinary things, boat wakes, windrows on the water, and the fact that a 127 km lake is mostly empty and always moving.

The fun part of the story is how the money piled up. A local tourism agency offered a cash reward for a proven sighting in the 1980s, and Greenpeace said the animal had to be filmed and not captured, which is how Ogopogo ended up listed as an endangered species as a joke. Nobody ever collected.

The statue in Kelowna City Park is the easy stop, and it's a good photo. Rattlesnake Island, also called Monster Island, is the spot the old accounts point to, along with the cliffs at Squally Point across the water. Both are on Syilx land and you don't just wander onto them, so look from the water or from the highway pullouts like everyone else.

If you want to try your luck, calm mornings off Peachland or the west side are where most of the modern reports come from. Bring binoculars and a healthy suspicion of your own eyes. I've watched a log for ten minutes and been completely sure.

faq.a: Nothing much, and that's the truth. The name comes from a 1924 British music hall song that was sung in Vernon, BC, with lyrics about a creature whose mother was an earwig and whose father was a whale. It's also a palindrome, which is why people joke that the creature looks the same from either end.

There's no record of Ogopogo hurting anybody. The old Syilx accounts are about a spirit that commanded respect and demanded an offering, and one story of a chief who refused and drowned with his family, but nobody has been attacked in the modern record. The 1855 story about a settler's horses being pulled into the lake is the closest thing to a casualty claim.

Yes, several times. Art Folden in 1968, Larry Thal in 1980, the Chaplins in 1989 and Paul DeMara in 1992 are the famous ones, and there's a 2008 photo from Peachland. Every one has been examined and explained as otters, a beaver, water birds, floating debris or a log. The Folden film looked strongest until researchers actually measured the distance to the object and shrank it.

Okanagan Lake in British Columbia, a 127 km lake between Vernon and Penticton. The old accounts put it near Rattlesnake Island, which locals call Monster Island, and the cliffs at Squally Point. Kelowna and Peachland are where most of the recent reports come from.

People compare it to a plesiosaur because of the long neck and humps, and others have compared it to Basilosaurus, an extinct whale. The problem is the same one every lake monster has. There need to be breeding animals, and a population that size in a lake this busy would leave something behind. Nobody has ever found a bone.

faq.q: What is Ogopogo called in the Okanagan language?
faq.a: N'ha-a-itk, written n'x̌x̌aitkʷ, which gets translated as water demon, water god or sacred creature of the water. The demon part is a translation problem according to people from Westbank First Nation, who describe the being as a protector of the valley rather than a monster.
